blocks.text: The photon reaches a molecule of chlorophyll.
A molecule is a group of atoms held together by chemical bonds. In chlorophyll, the arrangement of those atoms and their electrons allows it to absorb certain colours of light.
Its energy changes the electronic state of the molecule. The atoms remain linked, and the molecule still has the same number of electrons. But it now holds more electronic energy.
This is what it means to say that chlorophyll is excited.

blocks.label: Animation of photon absorption by chlorophyll
blocks.caption: Chlorophyll remains intact as its electronic energy increases.
blocks.description: A photon, represented by an orange wave packet, approaches a chlorophyll molecule and disappears when absorbed. The molecular drawing retains the same linked atoms. A separate electronic-energy indicator changes from a lower level to a higher level. The molecule is now in an excited state. This is a schematic, with time expanded to make the change visible.

blocks.text: Energy that travelled from the Sun has become an excitation in a molecule inside the leaf.
What happens to that energy next?

This is a temporary change.
The molecule can release energy as heat or emit a new photon.

But the pigments around it create another possibility.
They are close enough for the excitation energy to pass from one to another.

That is why their arrangement matters.
Together, they collect light and channel its energy towards a place where an electron can be passed to another molecule.
A reaction centre.
Passing on excitation energy and transferring an electron are two different steps.

No sugar has been made by this first step.
For now, light has changed the energy of a molecule.
What happens when that energy reaches the reaction centre?

notes.title: Where the light is caught
paragraphs: Many cells inside a leaf contain chloroplasts. Within each chloroplast, thylakoid membranes carry the protein complexes that collect light and carry out the first energy-conversion steps of photosynthesis.

Proteins hold chlorophyll and other pigments in particular positions and orientations. Their arrangement allows excitation energy to move through the light-harvesting network. The structure of a spinach light-harvesting complex provides a detailed example of this organisation.

sources.title: Liu et al. · Structure of the spinach light-harvesting complex

notes.title: What an excited state means
paragraphs: An electronic state describes the quantum state of a molecule’s electrons and its associated energy. The ground state has the lowest electronic energy; an electronically excited state has more.

Absorbing a suitable photon can promote chlorophyll to an excited electronic state. At this absorption step, the molecule has the same atoms and total number of electrons. An electron has not yet been transferred to another molecule.

A higher energy level is not a physical shelf or a planetary orbit. In a molecule, electrons occupy molecular orbitals that can extend across several atoms. The story follows the change in energy without assigning a classical path to an individual electron.

The animation uses a two-dimensional drawing based on chlorophyll a in the RCSB PDB Chemical Component Dictionary. Hydrogen atoms and the distinction between single and double bonds are omitted. The separate indicator shows electronic energy, not an electron’s position. The structure is held still for clarity; colours are illustrative and time is expanded to make the change visible.

sources.title: IUPAC Gold Book · Electronically excited state

notes.title: Why the colour of light matters
paragraphs: A photon’s energy depends on its frequency. For absorption, that energy must correspond to a transition available to the molecule: ΔE = hν. Here ΔE is the energy gained, h is Planck’s constant, and ν is the light’s frequency.

Chlorophyll’s molecular structure gives it strong absorption in red and blue regions of visible light. Green light is absorbed less strongly, so more can be reflected or transmitted. This contributes to a leaf’s green appearance; it does not mean green light can never be absorbed or used.

Real pigments absorb over bands of wavelengths. Molecular vibrations and interactions with their surroundings affect those bands. Matching an available transition makes absorption possible; it does not guarantee that every passing photon will be absorbed.

sources.title: RCSB PDB · Photosystem I and light absorption
Terashima et al. · How green light contributes to photosynthesis

notes.title: What can happen to the excitation
paragraphs: An excited state is temporary. Its energy may be dissipated as heat, emitted as a new photon through fluorescence, or transferred to neighbouring pigments. The emitted photon is a new photon; the absorbed one no longer exists.

In the antenna, excitation-energy transfer can occur without a net transfer of an electron from one pigment to the next. At a reaction centre, excitation enables a distinct event: an electron moves from a donor to an acceptor, creating separated electrical charges. This is the beginning of the subsequent electron-transfer chemistry.

One absorption event does not make a sugar molecule. Photosynthesis requires many light-driven events and further chemical reactions. The distinction here is between capturing light energy briefly and using it to drive those later steps.

sources.title: RCSB PDB · Photosystem II and antenna energy transfer
Larom et al. · Light harvesting, charge separation and electron transfer

introduction.heading: The race is tomorrow.
columns:
I’m sitting down to a plate of pasta.
But my mind is already running.

I see myself at the rolling start.
Moving closer.
Almost my turn.

I’m still at the dinner table.
But I can already feel it.
The adrenaline is high.

I replay the journey.
The training.
The moments that stayed with me.

Then I rehearse the transitions.
Step by step.

As I eat, I start putting it all on a timeline.
What brought me here.
What comes next.
closing: The sequence of events that makes this experience possible.
A story that starts long before race day.
